posts.text:
When does an AI web crawler cross the line from 'aggressive scraping' to an accidental DDoS? Last week's incident between OpenAI and Hugging Face gives us a textbook, albeit chaotic, answer.

Simon Willison’s timeline of OpenAI’s accidental "attack" on Hugging Face highlights a massive blind spot in how we deploy AI agents. This wasn't a malicious exploit. It was a runaway feedback loop. OpenAI’s systems hammered Hugging Face's infrastructure—specifically targeting Spaces and model repos—at a rate that looked exactly like a coordinated Layer 7 application DDoS.

The technical culprit? It points to runaway agentic behavior. When LLM-powered agents are given the autonomy to fetch live web resources but aren't configured with strict client-side rate limiting, exponential backoff, or circuit breakers, they fail catastrophically. Instead of backing off when hitting 429 Too Many Requests, these systems often do the opposite: they retry aggressively, turning a minor bottleneck into an infrastructure-crushing loop.

As security practitioners, we’ve spent years defending APIs against malicious actors. Now, we have to defend them against well-funded, clueless AI agents with massive compute behind them. If your API security model still relies on trusting well-known user-agents (like GPTBot) to behave responsibly by default, this incident is your wake-up call. 

Are we ready to treat LLM agents not just as automated users, but as unpredictable network traffic that requires zero-trust rate limiting? How is your team adapting your WAF rules for the age of agentic scraping?
posts.rationale: This topic was selected because it represents a highly relevant, real-world incident between two of the biggest players in the AI ecosystem (OpenAI and Hugging Face). It perfectly fits Ada's profile: it's highly technical, addresses an underreported angle of AI security (how agentic scraping behaves like a DDoS), and offers concrete architectural takeaways (rate limiting, backoff, WAF rules) rather than generic AI hype. It is timely, actionable, and appeals directly to AI security practitioners.
